seo.title: Karmic tail 6 11 5 compatibility: The Lovers, Strength, The Hierophant
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 11 5 compatibility: how a couple's wish to choose each other passes a trial of strength and becomes the couple's own law.

title: The 6-11-5 tail in compatibility: how a couple's love becomes its law
short: The karmic tail 6-11-5 in compatibility — The Lovers, Strength and The Hierophant — never occurs in a single person: in a personal destiny matrix it would need The Sun in the centre of the chart, and no one is born with The Sun there. Couples get it about one time in 32. It is the tail of a union that begins with the wish to choose each other, passes through a trial of strength and arrives at its main task: to write the couple's own law instead of living by someone else's rulebook.

sections.h2: What 6-11-5 means in a couple's destiny matrix
paragraphs: A couple has its own karmic tail: each of its points is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to a number from 1 to 22. Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the site uses to work out compatibility, calls this line the couple's tasks and says plainly that its trials may be called karmic or simply part of life. The line is read mostly through its minus — through what the couple fails at and has to learn.

The word "programme", which people type next to "6 11 5", comes from the same school: Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail a "karmic programme". She writes it from the main task, so in her book it appears as 5-11-6. Nor is it a random choice among many: when the author of the book on compatibility shows how to join the three energies of a tail into one conclusion, this is the triple she picks. Her analysis is a list of tasks, each marked with the combination of cards it comes from. Here it serves as a reference for what the points mean; the plot of this couple is its own.
The three points of the tail work like this:

ul: **entry to the task** — the couple's shared wishes and agreements, its "common language". The point sits on the relationship line, so what the couple wants together can also become what it resists with;

**middle of the task** — in Lisovskaya's book it has no meaning of its own and only complements the main point. We read it as the road: what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish to the task. This is the site's reading, not a statement of the book;
**main task** — the couple's main trials and what it has to learn.

paragraphs: **The first clue is in the names.** In the historical part of his book Arthur Edward Waite gives the sixth card a double name: "The Lovers or Marriage". And his divinatory list for The Hierophant opens with the same word — "Marriage". The 6-11-5 tail begins with marriage as a feeling and ends with marriage as an institution.

**The second clue is in the arithmetic.** 6 + 5 = 11. The middle of this tail is exactly the sum of its two ends: Strength here is made of The Lovers and The Hierophant, of love and law. What that means in practice is best seen in the tale.

sections.h2: The tale this couple lives in
paragraphs: "The Tale of Peter and Fevronia of Murom" was written by the monk Ermolai-Erasmus in the late 1540s at the request of Metropolitan Macarius. Peter and Fevronia are venerated as patrons of marriage, and since 2008 their feast day, 8 July, has been marked in Russia as the Day of Family, Love and Fidelity. Quotations from the tale below are our own translations from the Old Russian.
The plot rests on three acts, and each is one card of the tail:

ol: a prince and the daughter of a tree-climber make a deal: she will get him back on his feet if he takes her as his wife — **The Lovers**, choice and condition;
a serpent killed with a sword, and scabs taken away with sourdough — **Strength**, two kinds of strength in one story;
boyars, the law, and a stone coffin with a thin partition — **The Hierophant**, the question of whose rulebook governs this marriage.

paragraphs: The tale is not offered here as a model to copy, nor as a prediction. It is a mirror: in it one can see clearly how the three cards behave when they stand in a row.

sections.h2: The entry: The Lovers, or love with a condition
paragraphs: The prince's servant finds Fevronia in Laskovo, a village in the Ryazan lands. She is sitting at her loom, and a hare is leaping in front of her. The first thing he hears from her is a riddle: "It is unseemly for a house to be without ears and a temple without eyes." The servant does not understand. Fevronia explains: the ears of a house are a dog, which would have barked at a stranger; the eyes are a child, who would have seen the guest first. Her father and mother have gone "to weep on loan" — to a funeral, to weep for others so that one day others will weep for them. Her brother is a tree-climber who gathers wild honey; he looks down "through his legs into the land of the dead", so as not to fall.

So this union begins with a language not everyone understands. For a couple's tail that is no small thing. **The entry to the couple's task is its common language** — words and jokes that only two people get, agreements nobody else knows about. For a 6-11-5 couple this is where the road to the main task begins: pet names, private words, decisions like "with us it will be different from our parents".

Then comes the condition. The servant asks her to get the prince back on his feet. Fevronia answers that it can be done, but "if I am not to be his wife…" — then there is no reason for her to nurse him. Love here starts not with a sigh but with a contract spoken out loud. This is The Lovers as Benebell Wen reads the card: "in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice", and in matters of love it marks "the beginnings of romance and, simultaneously, the beginnings of temptation."

Temptation arrives at once. Hearing the condition, Peter thinks: "How can I, a prince, take a tree-climber's daughter as my wife!" He agrees for appearances' sake, and afterwards he sends gifts. The tale answers in three words: "She did not accept."

The whole minus of the entry is in this scene. The wish to be chosen argues with status, and a present arrives instead of a promise. Among the minuses of the six, Lisovskaya lists gifts given "with a calculation", and in her analysis of this tail — the chase after status. In a real couple it looks mundane: a new phone instead of the conversation that was asked for; weekend tickets instead of "I was wrong"; silence in front of the family instead of "yes, I choose you" — and flowers later. The gift is nice, but the condition was something else.
The roles of Peter and Fevronia are not handed out by sex. In a 6-11-5 couple either partner may be the one who sets the condition, and either may be the one who tries to pay with gifts.

sections.h2: The middle: Strength, or the sword and the sourdough
paragraphs: To understand the middle, one has to go back to the start of the tale. The prince's trouble began with a serpent. The serpent visited the wife of Peter's brother, Prince Paul of Murom, and to other people it looked like the prince himself, "as if the prince were sitting with his wife". A serpent wearing the face of the lawful husband — the same shadow that coils round the tree on The Lovers card: a desire that passes itself off as one's own.

Peter kills the serpent with the sword of Agrikov. It is a victory by force, and it wounds the victor: the serpent "sprinkled the blessed prince Peter with its blood", and from that blood the prince's body broke out in scabs and sores. The sword worked. The price was his skin.

Here Waite offers an unexpected hint. His description of Strength ends: "It has walked upon the asp and the basilisk and has trodden down the lion and the dragon." This is a verse of Psalm 91 — Psalm 90 in the Greek and Slavonic numbering — which in the Church Slavonic psalter reads "Thou shalt tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and trample the lion and the serpent". In Russia this psalm, known by its opening words Zhivyi v pomoshchi, "He that dwelleth in the help", is among the best known of all. So Strength has two faces: the one who tramples the serpent, and the one who leads the lion without a fight. **In the tale the two faces belong to two different people**: Peter has the sword, Fevronia has the sourdough.

Her remedy is deliberately ordinary. Fevronia "took a small vessel, scooped up some of her leaven and blew on it" — her bread sourdough and her breath. A quieter force is hard to imagine. And one condition: "and let him leave one scab unanointed." One scab must be left untouched.

Peter anointed himself, rose well again, broke his word — and "from that scab many scabs began to spread over his body". Everything came back from the one untouched spot. The prince returned in shame, and Fevronia repeated her condition: "If he is to be my husband, he will be made whole." This time he married her.

Fevronia is right: the scab is a pledge for the word. But in a couple this scene has a shadow. Sometimes each partner keeps "one scab in reserve" — an old hurt that was never spoken and never let go, kept just in case. It lies quiet while things are good and spreads in the first quarrel: "And remember the time you…" In her analysis of this tail Lisovskaya describes the same mechanism in other words: an unspoken "I don't like this" settles inside and grows like a weed — into insecurity, passive aggression, jealousy and manipulation.

The tale also has a third force — neither the sword nor submission. Before the wedding Peter decides to test her wisdom. He sends a bundle of flax with the order: "If she is wise, let her make me from this flax a shirt, trousers and a towel" — while he is in the bathhouse. Fevronia has a small piece cut from a log and sends it back: "let him first make me from this little stick a loom and all its fittings, on which his linen can be woven."

She neither argues nor obeys. She holds the demand up like a mirror: the impossible comes back as the impossible. Wen separates two neighbouring cards this way: The Chariot "is typically associated with the strength to master the world", while Strength "is associated with strength to master the self." And among the meanings of Strength reversed she names "being too stubborn and obstinate" — strength applied in the wrong place.

paragraphs.h3: A strength that belongs to neither partner

paragraphs: The strangest clue of this tail lies in the full run of dates. Strength never stands in the middle of a personal karmic tail: a check of every birth date since 1900 does not find it there once. So in a 6-11-5 couple the eleven in the middle is never brought by one partner — each time it is assembled from two other cards. One partner's Emperor and the other's Chariot (4 + 7). Judgement and The Hermit (20 + 9 = 29 → 11). Justice and The Empress (8 + 3). And in one such couple in six it is literally one partner's Hierophant and the other's Lovers, 5 + 6.
That is why this tail has no "born tamer". The couple's strength is shared; it arises between the two. Whoever starts taming the other is taking what belongs to both.

In daily life the middle of the tail shows up in arguments about big decisions — moving, a job, money. One partner presses with arguments as if with a sword. The other answers with sarcasm, and now there are two swords. Lisovskaya names this directly for the eleven: a struggle for leadership, each with a truth of their own. And the plus of the same card, in her book, is a fine sense of what the other needs, and a way of turning tension into passion rather than war. The strong move here resembles Fevronia's log: not "no" and not "fine", but "to do that, this is needed — let's start with the loom".

If strength in a couple has turned into fear, threats or physical violence, that is not "the task of the tail" and not a reason to endure. It is a reason to get help — from a local emergency number or a crisis line.

sections.h2: The main task: The Hierophant, or whose rulebook governs this marriage
paragraphs: After the wedding the longest trial begins. Peter becomes prince of Murom, and the boyars dislike the princess "because of her birth". The boyars' wives complain: she has a peasant habit — after a meal she gathers the crumbs from the table into her palm. Peter takes her hand, opens her fingers — and sees "fragrant incense and frankincense".

For the fifth card this is a precise scene. The Hierophant is the card of established order: how things are done, what is proper, who is an equal. The boyars' wives measure another man's wife by their own rulebook. And in her palm lies what is burned in church: the "low" habit turns out to be a rite as well — just not the one the court is used to.

Then the boyars speak plainly: "Let her take as much wealth as she likes and go wherever she wants!" Peter does not decide for her: "Say it to Fevronia, and whatever she says, we shall hear." Her answer: "I ask for nothing else but my husband, Prince Peter." The prince cites the words of the Gospel — that whoever puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery — and, in the tale's words, "did not love temporal rule above the commandments of God". The boyars give them boats on the Oka, and they sail away from their own city.

Here the two faces of The Hierophant collide. One is the norm of the court: who is fit to be princess. The other is the law of the union: the word that was given. **Peter uses the law to protect the couple from the norm.** That is the main task of the 6-11-5 tail: not to choose between love and order, but to make order serve the union instead of breaking it apart.

paragraphs.h3: Where it shows in a couple's life

paragraphs: Among the tasks of the five Lisovskaya names relatives meddling, even in the choice of a partner; conflict with the other's family; attempts to remake each other; lectures about how "everything is wrong". For a 6-11-5 couple the scenes are familiar:

ul: a holiday that "we have always spent at our place", with nobody asking where the two of them would like to spend it;
"that's not how it's done in our family" — the sentence by which someone else's rulebook walks into the shared home;
one partner becomes the other's high priest, teaching how to eat, dress, spend and talk, because "that's what normal people do";
the couple takes a ready-made template of marriage — their parents', a book's, other people's photos — and suffers because their union does not fit it.

paragraphs.h3: Water from both sides of the boat

paragraphs: On the same river there is a short scene. A man sailing in the same boat as Fevronia lets his eyes rest on her. She tells him to scoop up water from one side of the boat and drink it, then from the other side and drink again. "Is this water the same, or is one sweeter?" The same, he says. Then she finishes the lesson: what he was gazing at is no different either — so why leave what is his and think about what belongs to another?

For a 6-11-5 couple this scene holds the trap of comparison, and not only with other people. Someone else's marriage on the far side of the boat looks sweeter: everything there is by the book, their relatives never call, they never quarrel. Measuring one's own marriage by another's canon is the same as drinking from the other side.

In the evening the exiles make camp on the bank. The cook cuts thin saplings to hang the cauldrons on. Fevronia blesses them: "Let these be great trees by morning, with branches and leaves." In the morning, where the stakes stood, there are tall trees in full leaf.

This is the best image of where a couple's own rulebook comes from. Not from an inheritance and not from a book, but from the camping rules of two people in exile, made up in a hurry: where the pot goes, who does the dishes, what we do when we are scared. The temporary comes alive if nobody pulls it out.

Soon the same boyars come sailing after them: the city has torn itself apart in a fight for power — please come back. Peter and Fevronia return and rule, says the tale, "like a father and mother who love their children". This is the plus of the five in Lisovskaya's book: an authority everyone accepts willingly, not because that is the custom.

sections.h2: A thin partition: the ending that did not make the canon
paragraphs: In old age both take monastic vows: Peter under the name David, Fevronia as Euphrosyne. She is embroidering an altar cover with the faces of saints for the cathedral. Peter sends word that he is dying and waits for her, so that they may depart together. She answers: "Wait, my lord, until I finish the cover for the holy church." He sends a second time, then a third. Then she "thrust her needle into the cover and wound the thread round it" — and went.

Even the shared ending waited until she had finished her own work. In her analysis of this tail Lisovskaya writes separately that each partner needs a circle of like-minded people of their own and achievements they can see apart from the other. And among the pluses of the five she lists respect for personal space and support in which each grows in their own field.

Now the heart of it. The couple asked to be laid together and had an unusual tomb made for themselves: "in one stone two coffins, with only one partition between them". **One stone, one shared fate — and a thin wall, so each has a place of their own.** No closer formula for the main task of this tail exists: a union that does not swallow the two.

People decided otherwise: "it is not fitting to lay saints who have taken the monastic habit in one coffin". Peter was placed in a separate coffin in the city, Fevronia outside the city, in a convent. In the morning the separate coffins were empty, and both were found in the shared stone, in the city cathedral. They were moved apart once more — and again by morning they lay together. The rule of the institution lost to the rule of the couple.

The last clue lies not in the tale but in what happened to it. Macarius commissioned the text, and the council of 1547 numbered Peter and Fevronia among the saints, yet the Metropolitan left the tale out of the Great Menaion Reader, the main collection of saints' lives of the time; scholars explain this by its "exceptionally legendary" character. The institution accepted the saints and turned down their story: riddles, a hare, sourdough and empty coffins did not fit the canon. The couple held up as an example for almost five hundred years was never recognised as a model in form.

The Hierophant likes to turn a couple into a model — for others, for a holiday, for a photograph. The tale shows that this couple's real law was something else: a language of riddles, a condition spoken aloud, one stone for two and a thin partition inside.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: two unveiled, a lion on a chain of flowers, the keys
paragraphs: The cards on the site have their own artwork; this section is about the Waite–Smith deck of Arthur Edward Waite and Pamela Colman Smith.

**The Lovers.** In Waite the man and the woman stand "unveiled before each other". There is nothing to hide; in Lisovskaya's book the plus of the six includes having no secrets. Behind the woman stands the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, and "the serpent is twining round it". The tale of Murom begins with that serpent.

**Strength.** A woman is closing the jaws of a lion, and Waite adds what matters most: "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers." The struggle happened before the picture. The card shows what comes afterwards: the lion is held by a chain of flowers, which means that what holds him is not the strength of the chain.

**The Hierophant.** At the pontiff's feet lie the crossed keys, and two ministers kneel before him. Waite agrees with the writer who signed himself Grand Orient that this card is "the power of the keys". Keys bind and loose: who holds the keys to this marriage — the two of them, the relatives, or "society"? The divinatory list of the fifth card splits in two. Upright: "Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude". Reversed: "Society, good understanding, concord, over-kindness, weakness". The main task of the tail runs between captivity and concord. And there is a second boundary: concord that melts into "over-kindness" is no rulebook either.

sections.h2: The Sun in the centre: the person who cannot exist
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere between the partners, what is not on show. In couples with the 6-11-5 tail the centre holds one of two cards: The Sun (19) in 56.8% of them, The Wheel of Fortune (10) in 43.2%.

Here lies the answer to why this tail never occurs in a person. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre. For the entry to be 6 when the main task is 5, the centre would have to be 1 or 19: 5 + 19 = 24, 2 + 4 = 6. No person has a centre of 1 or 19: a personal centre can only be 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. **But a couple's centre can be 19 — and with it the 6-11-5 tail adds up exactly by the personal formula.** In more than half of these couples the union is built like a single person with The Sun in the centre — a person who cannot exist.

In his list for The Sun Waite writes: "Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment." And in older decks, he recalls, beneath the luminary there was a wall, "as it might be, a walled garden", with two children inside "gambolling, or running hand in hand". The card that no human being has in the centre once showed two.

In Lisovskaya's book The Sun in a couple's centre means respect, a cosy home, a sense of being safe next to the other; its minus is control and comparison. The Wheel of Fortune in the centre is the feeling of a fated meeting and a similar outlook on life; its minus is a seesaw of "silence, then conflict". Two atmospheres for one tail: a walled garden, and a wheel that lifts and lowers.

In the couple's values — the spiritual purpose — such unions have one of three cards: The Empress (3) in 48.3%, The World (21) in 33.8%, The Hanged Man (12) in 17.9%. The Empress, for Lisovskaya, is growth and abundance in whatever sphere the couple met for. The World is a shared philosophy of life, and among its pluses there is a detail that seems to continue the main task of the tail: the couple makes the budget rules together. The Hanged Man, in Waite, is "wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice": for the sake of what is shared, one sometimes has to look at one's own things upside down.

sections.h2: How to work out the 6-11-5 tail: an example couple
paragraphs: Take two dates: 08.01.1976 and 14.09.1975. First each personal matrix is worked out.

For 08.01.1976: day 8, month 1, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Main task 8 + 1 + 5 = 14, centre 8 + 1 + 5 + 14 = 28 → 10. Entry of the tail 14 + 10 = 24 → 6, middle 14 + 6 = 20. The personal tail is 6-20-14.
For 14.09.1975: day 14, month 9, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task 14 + 9 + 22 = 45 → 9, centre 14 + 9 + 22 + 9 = 54 → 9. Entry 9 + 9 = 18, middle 9 + 18 = 27 → 9. The personal tail is 18-9-9.
Now the couple's tail: each point is the sum of the same points.
The couple's centre is 10 + 9 = 19, The Sun. The couple's values are 21, The World.

The couple's middle is worked out from the partners' middles, not from the ends of the couple's tail. For 6-11-5 both ways happen to give the same result — 6 + 5 = 11 — but the rule is still one: the same points are added together.

The 6-11-5 tail occurs in about one couple in 32 — 3.1% — ninth among the 97 couple tails. It is assembled from 13 combinations of personal tails. The most common are 21-4-10 with 3-7-22 (16% of such couples), 15-20-5 with 9-9-18 (13%) and 15-8-11 with 18-3-12 (11%).

One more detail from the full run of dates: in two out of three couples with this tail, neither partner has The Lovers at their own entry or The Hierophant at their own main task. This triple is rarely brought by one person — two people make it.
No other couple tail is made of these three numbers. If the notation 5-11-6 turns up, it is the same tail read from the main task, as Lisovskaya writes it.
The tail passes no sentence and promises no events. It shows where this couple's knot lies. Here is what the tale and the cards suggest as a way out:

ul: **The condition — aloud and at the start.** Like Fevronia: not "if you loved me, you would guess", but "this is what I need". An agreement spoken plainly holds better than one that has to be guessed.
**No gifts in place of a word.** A present is fine in itself, but not instead of what was asked for.
**No scab kept in reserve.** Talk about a hurt while it is fresh, rather than storing it as a lever for the next quarrel.
**Meet pressure with a log.** Not with a sword and not with surrender, but with a counter-question: "to do that, this is needed".
**The keys to the union stay with the two.** In this home relatives are guests, not high priests.
**A rulebook of the couple's own.** A few rules both partners chose themselves — and the right to revise them. Stakes turn into trees if nobody pulls them out.
**A thin partition.** Each has a needle of their own: their own work, their own circle, their own time.
**Drinking from one's own side.** Someone else's marriage is not sweeter; it is just on the other side of the boat.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 6-11-5 tail
paragraphs: In its strong version this tail is the same tale, only told by two people for themselves. The couple starts with its own language and an honest condition, goes through the trial of strength without taking up the sword or keeping a scab in reserve, and writes a law nobody could have handed it: a shared stone with a thin wall inside. Such a union may not look like a model one — just as the tale of Peter and Fevronia does not look like a proper saint's life. But its rulebook is its own.

ul: **Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** Where the couple starts: choosing each other and coming to terms — a private language, conditions of its own, its own "we". The same wish later turns into resistance.
**Middle of the task — 11, Strength.** What the couple goes through: who holds whom, who nurses whom back, who tries to tame whom. This is where strength and power part ways.

**Main task — 5, The Hierophant.** What the couple has to learn: to turn love into a rulebook both of them accepted freely — not their parents', not "what normal people do", and not one written by one partner for the other.

intro: The best-known story of marriage in Old Russian literature is built exactly like this tail: in three acts, in the same order. What follows is an investigation — into what is written in the three cards, in the couple's numbers, and in a tale that has been read as a model of marriage for almost five hundred years and yet was never admitted into the great church collection of saints' lives.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-11-5 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, running from The Lovers through Strength to The Hierophant. The couple enters it through the wish to choose each other and come to terms, passes through a trial of strength — who holds and tames whom — and learns the main thing: to create the union's own rulebook instead of living by the rules of relatives, society or one of the partners.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail is read through its minus because it shows what the union has to learn, but it is never a verdict. The 6-11-5 tail does not say whether the relationship will last and does not predict events: it describes a knot this couple needs to untie — joining love and order so that order serves both partners.

faq.q: Can 6-11-5 appear in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and an entry of 6 with a main task of 5 needs a centre of 1 or 19. No person has such a centre. A couple can, and in 56.8% of couples with this tail the centre is exactly The Sun.

It isn't: it is one tail written from opposite ends. On the site a couple's tail is read from the entry to the main task: 6-11-5. Yuliana Lisovskaya, in her book on compatibility, writes it from the main task — 5-11-6. No other couple tail is made of these three numbers.

faq.q: Does The Hierophant on the main task mean the couple must get married?
faq.a: No. The Hierophant speaks of the law, tradition and order of a union, but it does not demand a marriage certificate, a church wedding or any particular form of relationship. The task is for the couple's rules to be accepted freely by both, rather than inherited from relatives or imposed by one partner on the other.

faq.q: What does "programme 6-11-5" mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: It is the same thing as the karmic tail 6-11-5. Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail a "karmic programme", and this is the very triple she chose in her book to show how the three energies of a tail are joined into one conclusion about the couple's tasks.

report.h3: The sword, the sourdough and one scab kept in reserve

Waite's description of Strength ends with a verse of Psalm 91: "It has walked upon the asp and the basilisk and has trodden down the lion and the dragon." The card has two faces — the one who tramples the serpent and the one who leads the lion without a fight. **In the tale the two faces belong to two different people: Peter has the sword, Fevronia has the sourdough.** She scooped up some of her bread leaven, blew on it and set one condition: "let him leave one scab unanointed."

Peter rose well again, broke his word — and everything came back from the one untouched spot. Fevronia is right: the scab is a pledge for the word. But the scene has a shadow. Sometimes each partner keeps **one scab in reserve** — an old hurt that was never spoken and never let go. It lies quiet while things are good and spreads in the first quarrel: "And remember that time…"

There is a third force too, neither the sword nor submission. Peter sends Fevronia a bundle of flax: if she is so wise, let her make him a shirt, trousers and a towel from it while he is in the bathhouse. She sends back a small piece of a log: let him first make a loom out of it. She neither argues nor obeys — the impossible comes back as the impossible.

The strangest clue of this tail: no person ever has Strength in the middle of a personal tail. In this couple the eleven is born each time from two other cards. So there is no born tamer here. Whoever starts taming the other is taking what belongs to both. If strength in a couple has turned into fear, threats or physical violence, that is not "the task of the tail" and not a reason to endure, but a reason to get help — from a local emergency number or crisis line.

The boyars' wives dislike a princess of humble birth: after a meal she gathers the crumbs into her palm. Peter opens her fingers — and sees fragrant incense. The "low" habit turns out to be a rite as well, just not the one the court is used to. The boyars offer her as much wealth as she likes if she will leave. Peter does not decide for her: "Say it to Fevronia, and whatever she says, we shall hear." She asks only for her husband. He cites the Gospel's words on keeping faith with one's wife — and sails away with her down the Oka, out of his own city.

Here the two faces of The Hierophant collide: the norm of the court and the law of the union. **Peter uses the law to protect the couple from the norm.** That is the main task of the tail: not to choose between love and order, but to make order serve both. In daily life it is the holiday "we have always spent at our place"; the sentence "that's not how it's done in our family"; a partner who has become the other's high priest, teaching how to eat, spend and talk.

On the river bank Fevronia blesses the thin saplings the cook has hung the cauldrons on, and by morning they stand as tall trees. A couple's own rulebook grows the same way: from the camping rules of two people, not from an inheritance. The temporary comes alive if nobody pulls it out.

report.h3: One stone and a thin wall

report: The couple asked to be laid "in one stone two coffins, with only one partition between them". **One stone for two and a thin wall, so each has a place of their own** — no closer formula for this tail exists. People decided that monks must not lie in one coffin and moved the bodies apart: one into the city, the other outside it. By morning both lay in the shared stone. The rule of the institution lost to the rule of the couple. And Metropolitan Macarius himself, who commissioned the tale, left it out of the main collection of saints' lives — scholars explain this by its "exceptionally legendary" character.
The strong version of the tail resembles this fate: the union may not look like a model one, but its rulebook is its own. What helps to get there:

ul: saying the condition aloud and at the start, rather than waiting for it to be guessed;
not replacing a word with gifts;
talking about a hurt while it is fresh, rather than keeping a scab in reserve;
meeting pressure with a log — a counter-question: "to do that, this is needed";
keeping the keys to the union with the two: relatives in this home are guests, not high priests;
leaving each partner their own work and their own circle — a thin wall inside the shared stone.
